previous_version: 1.1 (15 tasks, 3 milestones, all shipped; see shipped section)
scope: Tokitai v0.5.x -> v0.8.0: shipped pain-point remediation + 2026-Q2 research-driven next wave
philosophy_anchor: Preserve the in-process compile-time dispatch advantage while removing the rigidity, async friction, and ecosystem gaps that block broader adoption. Every new task must justify itself by exploiting the compile-time seam that runtime-only competitors cannot reach. Hard constraint: no dependency on `rmcp` or any other MCP SDK; spec is pinned via fixture + manual re-sync, not a moving dep.

differentiating_strategy.thesis: Tokitai is the only Rust tool-calling stack where schema and dispatch are produced by a proc-macro over a typed surface. That lets it solve seven classes of pain that runtime-only competitors cannot: schema-dialect fragmentation, tool-versioning drift, schema token-cost surprises, in-process observability, tool-description quality, declarative workflow composition, and per-tool result-size budget. Each new task in this file should be judged by whether it exploits the compile-time seam, not by whether it is 'a feature'.

pillars.pillar: Schema dialect correctness at compile time
pillars.pain_competitors_do_not_solve: `mcp-lint`, `tokitai-mcp-server` source bug, and every Python/Java team's runtime surprise: same JSON Schema, different provider, silent failure. mcp-lint only catches this post-hoc on saved specs; nothing catches it at the source.

pillars.pillar: Tool versioning as a type-system concern
pillars.pain_competitors_do_not_solve: Hard breaks when a tool is renamed or its arg shape changes. LangChain has ad-hoc `deprecated` markers; Anthropic's Claude Code has hand-rolled `aliases`. None of them have a compiler-checked lifecycle (deprecated_since / remove_in / replaced_by).
The 'burned 1000 tokens on a 128-tool prompt' surprise. OpenAI's hard cap, Claude Code's `shouldDefer` — both are workarounds for a measurement that Tokitai can compute at compile time for free.

`mcpdog` and Wireshark exist because the protocol is opaque. Tokitai's macro can splice in `tracing::instrument` spans that disappear entirely when the feature is off, so production hot paths pay zero.

pillars.pillar: Tool description quality as a compile-time lint (new)
pillars.pain_competitors_do_not_solve: Empirical numbers from production tool-call analyses (CSDN 2026-06): 47% parameter correctness with one-line desc, 68% with type hints, 80% with business context. Every framework treats the description as a free-form string; the quality of that string is a measurable lever nobody lints. The macro can score it at compile time and refuse to ship a description that scores below a threshold.

Every multi-step agent workflow (5+ tools chained) pays N round-trips of model latency and N copies of the tool schema. Anthropic's 'MCP code execution' pitch (98.7% token saving, 2025-11) works by collapsing the chain into a single tool, but it requires a separate sandbox. Tokitai can emit the same collapse at the macro level: `#[compose]` declares a multi-step workflow that expands to a single tool the LLM calls once.

pillars.pillar: Per-tool result-size budget at the wrapper, not at the LLM layer (new)
pillars.pain_competitors_do_not_solve: Production pain (CSDN 2026-06): 'one upstream API returned 8MB of unstructured JSON, the agent tried to process it, context blew up, retry loop fired 15 times, the whole system cascaded.' Headroom (2026-06) and the MCP code-execution pattern both attack this at the LLM-API layer. Tokitai can attack it at the tool boundary — `#[tool(result_truncate_bytes = 4096)]` compiles a runtime guard into the wrapper, so a single tool cannot blow the context regardless of what the LLM-side layer does.

pillars_we_reject: Becoming a second MCP SDK. We do not chase spec-conformance market share; rmcp does that. Hard rule reaffirmed: no rmcp or any other MCP SDK as a dependency.
Runtime plugin / hot-reload as a first-class model. It conflicts with the compile-time schema pillar; we add a non-default `DynamicToolProvider` trait instead (T-010, shipped).
LLM-provider SDK features (streaming, prompt caching, context-window math). Tokitai's job ends at `call_tool`.
Replacing the macro pipeline (syn/quote -> something else). All changes are additive or surgical.
Adding features with no test surface. Every task in the new wave ships with a fixture / test / trybuild entry.

non_goals: Become a second rmcp - hardcoded NO. T-005 implements stdio MCP directly; the rule extends to all new tasks.
Rewrite the macro pipeline (syn/quote -> something else). All changes below are additive or surgical.
Add features that have no test surface.
Match the LLM-side harness surface (LangChain's `AgentExecutor`, AutoGen's groups, CrewAI's crews). Tokitai is below that layer.

ci_status_at_2026-06-19.cargo_test_all_features: PASS (0 failed across all suites; trace_feature 3/3, provider_envelope 12/12, tool_versioning 13/13, error_injection 34/34, integration 7/7)

new_pain_points_2026_q2.title: Tool description quality is a measurable lever but no compile-time linter exists
new_pain_points_2026_q2.evidence: CSDN production-engineering post-mortem (2026-06-10, '我在生产环境踩的那些LLM Tool Calling 坑'): measured 1000 actual tool calls; parameter correctness was 47% with one-line desc, 68% with type hints, 80% with business context. Every framework (LangChain, Spring AI, MCP, Anthropic) treats the description as a free-form string. There is no compile-time check that the string is dense enough.
new_pain_points_2026_q2.impact: The macro emits the description into the JSON schema that the LLM sees on every turn (CSDN 2026-05 'context poisoning' article: '如果你有十个服务器每个 10-30 个工具,加起来就是几百条自然语言描述,每一轮对话 agent 都得把它们重新解析一遍'). A bad description makes the situation worse on both axes.
new_pain_points_2026_q2.first_mover_opportunity: Tokitai's macro can lint the `desc = "..."` literal at compile time and refuse to ship an underspecified one. Other stacks see this only post-hoc in the call logs.

new_pain_points_2026_q2.title: Multi-step workflows pay N round-trips and N copies of the schema, with no composition primitive
new_pain_points_2026_q2.evidence: CSDN 2025-11-29: 'AI Agent 架构革命: MCP 代码执行实现 98.7% Token 优化'. Anthropic's published claim: by collapsing N tool calls into a single tool executed inside a code sandbox, you save 98.7% of tokens and reduce wall-clock latency. The 2026 framework comparison (2026-04) shows every major agent framework (LangGraph, AutoGen, OpenAGI) treats multi-step composition as a runtime control-flow concern, not a schema concern.
new_pain_points_2026_q2.impact: Every agent with a 5-step workflow pays: 5x model latency, 5x prompt tokens for the tool list, 5x chance of a cascading error (one tool failure breaks the chain - Evidently AI's 2026 framing).
new_pain_points_2026_q2.first_mover_opportunity: A `#[compose]` macro that declares a multi-step workflow as a single tool, expanded by the proc-macro, would collapse the round-trip count without any sandbox - the call is still in-process Rust. The LLM sees one tool, the runtime executes the chain. This is the same token saving as Anthropic's code-execution pattern, with zero infrastructure.

new_pain_points_2026_q2.title: Tool result size is unbounded; 8MB JSON from one tool can blow the context and cascade into infinite retry
new_pain_points_2026_q2.evidence: CSDN 2026-06-10 production post-mortem: 'one upstream API returned 8MB of unstructured JSON, the agent tried to process it, context blew up, the retry strategy had no backoff, the same request fired 15 times, downstream rate limit tripped, the whole system cascaded.' Headroom (2026-06) addresses this at the LLM-API layer; the MCP code-execution pattern (2025-11) addresses it by moving the data outside the prompt.
new_pain_points_2026_q2.impact: A single tool can take down the whole agent regardless of how good the LLM-side guardrails are, because the data enters the agent's context window before the LLM sees it.
new_pain_points_2026_q2.first_mover_opportunity: The macro can compile a per-tool result-size budget into the wrapper (`#[tool(result_truncate_bytes = 4096)]`). The wrapper truncates BEFORE returning to the LLM, so a single tool's contract is enforced regardless of what the upstream returns. This is cheaper and more local than every LLM-layer solution.

new_pain_points_2026_q2.title: No typed way to evolve tool schemas across versions; breaking changes look identical to additive ones at the dispatcher
new_pain_points_2026_q2.evidence: CSDN 2026-04 'AIAgent 架构版本演进': cross-version agent frameworks need a compatibility matrix (state serialization format, tool call protocol, memory interface) and require users to run `aiagent migrate --from=v1.8 --to=v2.4` and hand-author adapter shims. MCP itself has no concept of schema evolution; every server just revs and breaks clients.
new_pain_points_2026_q2.impact: When a tool's signature changes from `query_db(sql: String)` to `query_db(sql: String, limit: Option<u32>)`, the old LLM clients keep calling it with one arg, get a validation error, and the agent's success rate drops silently.
new_pain_points_2026_q2.first_mover_opportunity: T-013 already handles the `replaced_by` rename case. The next layer is `since` / `until` per schema version: a typed diff that the dispatcher uses to serve the right `ToolDefinition` for the current `tokitai_core::current_version()`. Adding an optional field is non-breaking; removing a field or changing a type is breaking and the macro can refuse to compile across an incompatible pair.

new_pain_points_2026_q2.title: MCP has known RCE design flaws; every tool handle is a shell-injection sink
new_pain_points_2026_q2.evidence: QQ news 2026-04-18: 'Anthropic 创建、维护的行业标准 AI 通信协议 MCP 存在设计缺陷,可导致服务器被诱导执行任意代码 (RCE)'. CVE-2025-59377 (2025-09-25) on `mcp-kubernetes-server`: 'through 0.1.11 allows OS command injection via /mcp/kubectl endpoint ... executes it with subprocess using shell=True, enabling injection through shell metacharacters'. Multiple CWE-78 disclosures on `docker-mcp-server`, `code-screenshot-mcp`, etc. The flaw is architectural: the tool handler's input string is concatenated into a shell command or eval'd before any schema validation.
new_pain_points_2026_q2.impact: Any consumer of an MCP server is one malformed request away from RCE. Schema validation happens AFTER the sink, not before.
new_pain_points_2026_q2.first_mover_opportunity: Tokitai can generate a typed Rust wrapper around every MCP tool that validates args against the JSON schema BEFORE the call. The wrapper has a typed `fn call(args: ToolArgs) -> Result<ToolResult, ToolError>` surface, not a JSON passthrough. Catches type-confusion attacks at compile time (the schema is enforced) and at runtime (the typed deserializer refuses malformed input). This is defense-in-depth that rmcp / the official SDKs do not provide.

new_pain_points_2026_q2.title: Tool examples are hand-curated JSON in a separate file; they drift from the real signature
new_pain_points_2026_q2.evidence: Anthropic's tool-use best-practices (2025-2026): 'include 1-3 examples in the schema's `examples` field'. OpenAI function-calling guide: same recommendation. In every existing stack (LangChain, Spring AI, MCP servers), the example is a hand-maintained JSON literal that lives next to the function but not in the same source file. When the function's signature changes, the example rots silently and the LLM sees an example that doesn't match the actual contract.
new_pain_points_2026_q2.impact: Examples that contradict the real signature actively make tool-call reliability worse than no example at all (the LLM copies the wrong shape).
new_pain_points_2026_q2.first_mover_opportunity: A `#[tool(example = call!(foo(1, 2) => 3))]` attribute on a method would let the user write the example as a Rust expression that uses the same types as the real signature. The macro evaluates the expression at compile time and serializes the (args, result) pair into the schema's `examples` field. The example can never drift from the signature because both come from the same type. Nobody else does this; the closest competitor is `ts-rest`'s contract types, and even that is hand-maintained.

new_tasks.title: Bake few-shot examples into the schema as Rust expressions (kill hand-maintained JSON examples)
new_tasks.north_star: Tool examples are part of the function, not a separate JSON file. They cannot drift from the signature because they are the signature.
new_tasks.rationale: Anthropic + OpenAI both recommend 1-3 examples in the schema's `examples` field. Every existing framework ships the example as a hand-maintained JSON literal that lives in a different file from the function. When the signature changes, the example rots silently and hurts reliability. Tokitai's macro can accept `#[tool(example = call!(foo(1, 2) => 3))]` - a Rust expression using the same types as the real method - and evaluate it at compile time. The example can never drift. Unique to the typed compile-time surface: the LLM side has no equivalent.
acceptance_criteria: `#[tool(example = call!(self.add(1, 2) => 3))]` on a method emits a schema whose `examples` field contains `{ 'input': { 'a': 1, 'b': 2 }, 'output': 3 }`.
The macro rejects the example at compile time if the call's input or output type does not match the real method's signature (so a stale example cannot ship).

`tokitai-macros/tests/example_baking_test.rs` covers: positive (3 cases), negative where the example's type does not match (2 cases that compile-fail with a span at the `example =` literal), and one case proving the example appears in `to_openai_function()` / `to_anthropic_tool()` / `to_mcp_tool()` output.
`docs/AI_INTEGRATION.md` gains a 'Why bake examples' section with a benchmark claim sourced from the CSDN 2026-06 production post-mortem.
open_questions: Q-6: How many examples per tool? Default to 1 (the user wrote it explicitly), but allow `examples = [call!(...), call!(...)]`?

Q-7: Does the macro need a sandboxed evaluator, or is it always the host crate's normal Rust types? (Recommended: always host types. The expression lives in the user's code, so it cannot execute at macro time anyway - the macro sees the call site as a TokenStream and inlines the literal args/result the user wrote.)

new_tasks.title: Declarative multi-step tool composition: #[compose] collapses N tool calls into 1 (kill the 98.7% token waste)
new_tasks.north_star: The LLM sees one tool. The runtime executes the chain. Same in-process safety as a single call.
new_tasks.rationale: Anthropic's MCP code-execution pattern (CSDN 2025-11-29) saves 98.7% tokens by collapsing N tool calls into a single tool executed inside a code sandbox. The sandbox is the part that costs engineering. Tokitai can do the same collapse without a sandbox because the steps are in-process Rust method calls: `#[compose(name = "book_trip", steps = [search_flights, filter_by_price, book_flight, send_email])]` expands to a single `__call_book_trip` that the LLM calls once, and the wrapper calls the four sub-tools in sequence. The LLM's tool list shrinks by N-1 entries. Unique because no runtime-only competitor can make this work without either (a) a separate sandbox like Anthropic's, or (b) hand-rolled glue code that lives in the user's repo instead of the macro.
acceptance_criteria: `#[compose(name = "book_trip", steps = [search_flights, filter_by_price, book_flight, send_email])]` on an `impl` block expands to a single tool the LLM calls once, with a JSON schema whose `args` are the union of the first step's `args` and whose `result` is the last step's `result`.

Composition is enforced at compile time: the macro checks that every named step method exists on the same `impl` block, that the input types chain (output of step N must satisfy the input type of step N+1's first non-self arg), and that the composition is acyclic.

`tokitai/tests/compose_test.rs` covers: a 4-step pipeline where each step has a non-trivial signature, a 2-step pipeline where the intermediate type is a custom struct, and one negative case where the chain's types do not connect (compile-fail at the `steps = [...]` span).
`docs/AI_INTEGRATION.md` gains a 'Composing tools' section with a token-savings table: 1-call vs 4-call (schema bytes, prompt tokens, wall-clock latency) for a realistic example.
Backwards-compatible: existing `#[tool]` impls without `#[compose]` are unaffected. `#[compose]` is a new attribute on `impl Tool for X` blocks.
open_questions: Q-8: Does `#[compose]` support parallel steps (`steps = [[a, b], c]`) or only sequential? Parallel requires `tokio::join!` in the wrapper and is gated on `tokitai_core::current_async_executor()` being Some. Recommend: v1 is sequential only; parallel is a v2 stretch that depends on T-003's executor registry.

new_tasks.title: Compile-time description quality linter (kill the 47% / 68% / 80% accuracy gap)
new_tasks.north_star: A `desc = "..."` literal that does not score above the threshold is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
new_tasks.rationale: CSDN 2026-06-10 production post-mortem measured 1000 tool calls: parameter correctness was 47% with one-line desc, 68% with type hints, 80% with business context. Every framework treats the description as free-form text. The macro can compute a quality score at compile time from the literal (length, presence of 'returns' / 'side-effect' / 'requires' / 'throws' keywords, presence of a noun phrase for the action, presence of a unit or type hint, and the sentence count). Below a threshold (default: 60/100) -> `compile_error!` with a span at the `desc =` literal and a suggestion. The user can opt out with `#[tool(desc = "...", allow_short_desc)]` for the rare case where brevity is the point (e.g. one-word verbs). Unique to compile-time: the lint runs once and never runs again.
acceptance_criteria: `#[tool(desc = "adds")]` (3 chars, no type hint, no business context) fails to compile with a span at the `desc =` literal and a 'description scores 25/100; minimum is 60/100' message. `#[tool(desc = "Adds two 32-bit integers and returns their sum as i32. Requires both operands to be in the i32 range; returns Err on overflow.")]` passes.

The score is computed by a const fn in `tokitai-macros/src/description/score.rs` over the literal token tree. The four signals: length, type/unit hint, business-context keywords, sentence count. Each contributes 0-25 points. The threshold is `#[tool(min_desc_score = 60)]` (default 60, can be lowered or raised per impl).
`tokitai-macros/tests/description_score_test.rs` has 10 cases: 5 pass, 3 fail with a span at the literal, 2 use `allow_short_desc` to opt out.
`docs/AI_INTEGRATION.md` gains a 'Writing tool descriptions that score well' section with the 4 signals and the empirical 47% / 68% / 80% numbers from CSDN 2026-06 as the motivation.
Zero runtime cost: the score is computed at macro time and produces a `compile_error!` or nothing. The literal string is otherwise untouched.

new_tasks.title: Per-tool result-size budget: #[tool(result_truncate_bytes = N)] compiles a runtime guard into the wrapper
new_tasks.north_star: A single tool's contract is enforced at the tool boundary, regardless of what the upstream returns.
new_tasks.rationale: CSDN 2026-06-10 production post-mortem: 'one upstream API returned 8MB of unstructured JSON, the agent tried to process it, context blew up, the whole system cascaded.' Headroom (2026-06) and the MCP code-execution pattern both attack this at the LLM-API layer. Tokitai can attack it at the tool boundary: `#[tool(result_truncate_bytes = 4096)]` compiles a runtime guard into the wrapper. If the serialized result exceeds 4096 bytes, the wrapper truncates with a `...[truncated at 4096 bytes, original was X bytes]` sentinel and emits a `tracing::warn!` (using T-015's trace feature if on). The LLM sees a bounded payload regardless of upstream behavior. Cheaper and more local than every LLM-layer solution, and it composes with T-015 (the truncation event is itself a span).
acceptance_criteria: `#[tool(result_truncate_bytes = 4096)]` on a method whose return value serializes to 8000 bytes produces a truncated result with a sentinel `...[truncated at 4096 bytes, original was 8000 bytes]` and emits `tracing::warn!` if the `trace` feature is on.

If the return type is a UTF-8 string, truncation respects codepoint boundaries (no mid-codepoint cut). For arbitrary `Serialize` types, the macro emits `serde_json::to_vec` + byte-level truncation + parse back into the original type with a best-effort recovery (the truncated JSON may fail to deserialize; the wrapper returns `ToolError::Truncated { original_bytes, kept_bytes }`).
Default is unlimited (backwards compatible). Setting `result_truncate_bytes = 0` is a compile error (the sentinel would consume the whole output).
`tokitai/tests/result_truncate_test.rs` covers: string truncation at a UTF-8 boundary, struct truncation via JSON parse, a `tracing` test proving the warn span fires, and a 0-byte compile-fail case.
`docs/AI_INTEGRATION.md` adds 'Bounding tool result size' with the CSDN 2026-06 production post-mortem as the motivating case.

new_tasks.title: Typed schema evolution: #[tool(since = "1.0", until = "2.0")] + current_version() dispatch
new_tasks.north_star: Breaking schema changes between versions are compile errors, not silent agent failures.
new_tasks.rationale: T-013 handles the `replaced_by` rename case. The remaining pain is the additive-vs-breaking distinction: adding an optional field is non-breaking across versions, but removing a field or changing a field's type is breaking. The CSDN 2026-04 'AIAgent architecture evolution' article shows every major framework treats this as a hand-rolled migration step (`aiagent migrate --from=v1.8 --to=v2.4`). Tokitai can do better: when two `#[tool(since = ...)]` intervals overlap incompatibly (e.g. a field removed in 2.0 is still required by 1.x's `since = 1.0`), the macro refuses to compile the consumer's `tokitai_core::set_current_version("1.5")` against the 2.0 schema. The current schema is the one the dispatcher serves. Compatible with T-013's `replaced_by`: an old tool that was `replaced_by` a new one in 2.0 routes through the T-013 redirect, no separate handling needed.
acceptance_criteria: `#[tool(since = "1.0", until = "2.0")]` and `#[tool(since = "2.0")]` on two methods in the same impl block compile cleanly. Calling `set_current_version("1.5")` exposes only the 1.0 method; `set_current_version("2.0")` exposes only the 2.0 method.

If a 1.0 method removes a field that 2.0's `set_current_version("2.0")` consumer still calls, the macro emits a compile error pointing at the removed field's span. (Detected via the macro reading the consumer crate's `tokitai_core::current_version()` constant at compile time. If absent, only the 2.0 method is served.)

A SemVer-ordered comparison is performed: `since = "1.10.0"` < `until = "2.0.0"` is true; `since = "2.0.0"` < `until = "2.0.0"` is false. Loose strings are accepted (CalVer, commit SHA) but disable the typed-diff feature with a `compile_error!` recommending `version_policy = "semver"`.

`tokitai/tests/schema_evolution_test.rs` covers: additive change (new optional field) is non-breaking, breaking change (removed required field) is a compile error when `current_version()` predates the change, version-policy `"semver"` enforces ordered comparisons.
`docs/API_STABILITY.md` is extended with a 'Schema evolution' section that links T-013's `replaced_by` and T-020's `since/until` as a coherent versioning story.
open_questions: Q-5 (existing, re-applicable): Should `since` / `until` accept any string, or require `version_policy = "semver"`? Recommendation: accept any string, opt into semver for typed comparison. Documented in T-013 already.

new_tasks.title: Typed MCP handle layer: defense-in-depth against the RCE class of MCP vulnerabilities (no rmcp)
new_tasks.north_star: Every MCP tool the consumer imports is a typed Rust function. The JSON schema is enforced before the call reaches the handler.
new_tasks.rationale: QQ news 2026-04-18: 'Anthropic 创建、维护的行业标准 AI 通信协议 MCP 存在设计缺陷,可导致服务器被诱导执行任意代码 (RCE)'. CVE-2025-59377 (2025-09-25) on mcp-kubernetes-server: shell injection via the /mcp/kubectl endpoint. The architectural flaw: tool handlers receive unvalidated JSON strings and pass them to `subprocess.run(shell=True)`. The fix is to enforce the JSON schema BEFORE the call reaches the handler, with a typed Rust surface. Tokitai can generate this layer: for every tool defined in an MCP server the consumer trusts, the macro emits `fn call(args: TypedArgs) -> Result<TypedResult, ToolError>` where `TypedArgs` / `TypedResult` are derived from the tool's `inputSchema` (already in the source). The handler is wrapped: the JSON is deserialized to `TypedArgs` first; if the deserialization fails, the call is refused with `ToolError::ValidationError`. This catches type-confusion attacks (the LLM supplies a string where the schema says integer) before the handler ever runs. **No rmcp dependency** - the typed layer sits on top of the stdio/HTTP transport that T-005 already implemented, just with a different trust boundary.
acceptance_criteria: For an MCP server whose `tools/list` response is a fixture in `tokitai-mcp-server/tests/fixtures/mcp-spec/`, the macro generates `pub fn call_<tool_name>(args: <TypedArgs>) -> Result<<TypedResult>, ToolError>` for each tool. `TypedArgs` / `TypedResult` are generated from the tool's `inputSchema` and `outputSchema`.

A malformed call (e.g. an integer field receives a string) is rejected at the typed boundary with `ToolError::ValidationError`, with the path to the offending field in the error message. The handler is never called.

The typed layer is enabled by `tokitai = { features = ["mcp-typed"] }` (off by default - the JSON-passthrough path is preserved for backward compat and for cases where the consumer explicitly wants the legacy trust model).

`tokitai-mcp-server/tests/mcp_typed_layer_test.rs` covers: a positive call against each fixture tool, a negative call that supplies the wrong type and asserts `ToolError::ValidationError` with no handler invocation (handler call count is asserted via a counter), and a fuzz case that runs 100 random input shapes against each tool and asserts every malformed input is refused.

`docs/MCP_ARCHITECTURE.md` gains a 'Typed handle layer (T-021)' section that positions the feature as a defense-in-depth against the CVE-2025-59377 class of bugs. **Cargo.toml adds NO dependency on rmcp or any MCP SDK** (hard rule reaffirmed).
Backwards-compatible: `tokitai-mcp-server` with no `mcp-typed` feature behaves identically to today (JSON passthrough). The typed layer is opt-in.

new_milestones.label: Compile-time moats for description quality, composition, and result size
exit_criteria: Every `#[tool(desc = "...")]` literal is scored at compile time; below the default threshold, the macro refuses to compile (T-018).
Every `#[tool]` method can carry a baked few-shot example as a Rust expression; the example is in the schema's `examples` field and cannot drift from the signature (T-016).
Multi-step agent workflows can be declared as a single `#[compose]` tool that the LLM calls once; the wrapper executes the chain in-process (T-017).
Every `#[tool]` method can declare a `result_truncate_bytes = N` budget; the wrapper enforces the bound before the result reaches the LLM (T-019).

Schema evolution is typed: `since` / `until` intervals overlap-checked at compile time, `current_version()` dispatch serves the right schema, breaking changes across versions are compile errors (T-020).

MCP tools imported into tokitai-mcp-server can be wrapped in a typed Rust handle layer (`mcp-typed` feature) that enforces the JSON schema before the call reaches the handler, defending against the CVE-2025-59377 class of bugs (T-021). **No rmcp dependency.**

new_open_design_questions.question: How many examples per tool?
new_open_design_questions.context: Anthropic recommends 1-3 examples per tool. Should the macro accept `example = call!(...)` (one) or `examples = [call!(...), call!(...)]` (array)?
new_open_design_questions.recommendation: Accept both. Default to the singular form. The plural form is sugar over an array literal.

new_open_design_questions.question: Does the `#[tool(example = ...)]` macro evaluate the example at macro time, or just embed it?
new_open_design_questions.context: If the macro evaluates the example (runs the call), the example must be a pure const expression - the user's types may not have const constructors. If the macro just embeds the literal args + literal result the user wrote, the example is not 'live' but is always type-checked.
new_open_design_questions.recommendation: Embed, do not evaluate. The macro sees the call site as a TokenStream, inlines the literal args + literal result the user wrote, and runs the type checker to make sure they match the real signature. No runtime cost, no const-expr requirement.

new_open_design_questions.question: Should `#[compose]` support parallel steps?
new_open_design_questions.context: Sequential chains are the v1 target. Parallel steps would require `tokio::join!` in the wrapper and gate on `tokitai_core::current_async_executor()` being Some.
new_open_design_questions.recommendation: Sequential only for v1. Parallel is a v2 stretch that depends on T-003's executor registry. Mark as a tracked enhancement under T-017's followups.
